rashi:a1.1: We found wine and oil: that one does not tithe from one for the other, since “best” is written for each one.
rashi:a1.2: Wine and grain: of which only one “best” is written for the two of them; from where do we derive that one may not separate teruma from grain for wine, or from wine for grain?
rashi:a1.3: Grain and grain: wheat for barley and barley for wheat. Vines and olives are not diverse kinds with each other; grain with grain is diverse kinds of seeds by rabbinic law; grain with wine [i.e., grain sown among vines] is diverse kinds of the vineyard by Torah law. [Tosafot below argue that “by rabbinic law” here is a scribal error.]
tosafot:a1.1: And if wine and oil, which are not diverse kinds with each other, etc.: From new and old [produce] we cannot make an a fortiori inference in this way, “If new and old, which are not diverse kinds with each other [may not be tithed one for the other],” because one could reply: let the tithe of sheep and goats prove otherwise, since they are diverse kinds with each other and yet are tithed one for the other; so too I will bring wine and grain, grain and grain. And if you say: now too, when he makes the a fortiori inference from wine and oil, let sheep and goats of the animal tithe still prove otherwise! One can say that the refutation does not apply, because in animal tithe we do not find things of a single year that are not diverse kinds and yet may not be tithed one for the other, as we find in the tithe of grain, where wine and oil of a single year are not diverse kinds and are not tithed one for the other. But against an a fortiori inference from new and old the refutation is more fitting, since in animal tithe too we find new and old, which are not diverse kinds and are not tithed one for the other, while sheep and goats, which are diverse kinds with each other, are tithed one for the other.
tosafot:a1.2: In brief: Rashi’s commentary says that diverse kinds of seeds, grain with grain, are rabbinic; Tosafot think this is a scribal error. Here the Gemara implies it is Torah law, and so it is shown in Kiddushin 39a and Ḥullin 115a, where the Gemara asks that diverse kinds of seeds should be forbidden [to eat] as something “I have made abominable to you”; the only difference between diverse kinds of the vineyard and diverse kinds of seeds is that the latter may be eaten while the former is forbidden even for benefit. Even Rabbi Yoshiya holds that diverse kinds of seeds applies, making one liable for wheat and barley alone; the Gemara here says “by means of something else” for him because of wine and grain, since for diverse kinds of the vineyard he makes one liable only with three kinds, while for diverse kinds of seeds two suffice. They prove this from Ḥullin 82b (“there are two types of diverse kinds,” to exclude Rabbi Yoshiya, teaching that wheat with a grape seed, or barley with a grape seed, also makes one liable), discussing the variant readings there, and from the Jerusalem Talmud (Kilayim, chapter 8), where Rabbi Yoshiya and Rabbi Yonatan expound “your field” and “your vineyard”: both make one liable for diverse kinds of seeds with two kinds, and they disagree only about the vineyard, where Rabbi Yoshiya requires two kinds of seed together with the grape seed and Rabbi Yonatan only one. It is not strange that Rabbi Yoshiya requires three kinds in the vineyard, since he reads “diverse kinds” as two kinds of seed, and a grape seed is not a kind of seed. Rabbi Yehuda, however (Mishna Kilayim 1:9), seems to require three kinds even for diverse kinds of seeds, though he cannot read the verse about crossbreeding animals that way. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
gershom:a1.1: We found wine and oil, [and] grain and oil: since “best” is written for this one and “best” for that one, to say that one does not tithe from one for the other. Wine and grain, where “best” is not written for grain: from where do we derive that one does not tithe from one for the other?
rashi:a2.1: And according to Rabbi Yoshiya, who says: grain and wine are not diverse kinds, and grain and grain are not diverse kinds, until one sows all three together with a single hand motion.
rashi:a2.2: How does he derive it: by the a fortiori inference?
gershom:a2.1: Who says: wheat, barley and a grape seed with a single hand motion, and not with the oxen [our rendering of this phrase is tentative]. For now you cannot say that wine and grain, or grain and grain, are diverse kinds, since it is not diverse kinds until there are wheat, barley and a grape seed. How do they derive it by the a fortiori inference?
rashi:a3.1: Even by means of something else: for if one sowed a third kind [with them], either wheat or barley, they are not diverse kinds, since there must be two kinds of grain and a kind of the vineyard.
rashi:a3.2: Wine and grain: which are two kinds that become diverse kinds by means of a third kind; or grain and grain, which become diverse kinds by means of the vine: is it not logical, etc.
gershom:a3.1: Even by means of something else: if one adds another kind to them, wheat or barley, it is not diverse kinds; even so, one does not tithe from one for the other.
tosafot:a5.1: [Sefaria prints this Tosafot a second time here, on Rabbi Yoshiya’s “by means of something else”; its text is the same as the Tosafot on “grain and grain, which are diverse kinds” above.] In brief: Rashi’s statement that diverse kinds of seeds are rabbinic seems to be a scribal error; the Gemara here, Kiddushin 39a and Ḥullin 115a show it is Torah law. Even Rabbi Yoshiya makes one liable for diverse kinds of seeds with two kinds alone; “by means of something else” is said because of wine and grain, since for diverse kinds of the vineyard he requires three kinds. This is shown from Ḥullin 82b and from the Jerusalem Talmud (Kilayim, chapter 8), where Rabbi Yoshiya requires two kinds of seed with the grape seed and Rabbi Yonatan one; Rabbi Yehuda (Mishna Kilayim 1:9) requires three kinds even for diverse kinds of seeds. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
rashi:a4.1: And two species in general: that are not grain, such as beans and lentils; from where do we derive that they are not tithed from one for the other?
rashi:a4.2: These: all the other species are rabbinic, since by Torah law only grain, wine and oil are subject to tithe; and whatever they instituted, they instituted parallel to Torah law, [so] they instituted that they not be tithed from one species for another that is not its species.
tosafot:a4.1: In brief: This implies that every species not written in this verse [grain, wine and oil] is subject to tithes only by rabbinic law, as is said elsewhere: tithe of the caper is rabbinic (Berakhot 36a); “an item that is counted is not nullified even in a thousand” was said of rabbinic law, regarding a litra of dried figs (Beitza 3b); tithe of ordinary carobs is rabbinic (Rosh HaShana 15b), although the Sifrei discusses which carobs are exempt. All the expositions of the Sifrei that include legumes, tree fruit and vegetables in tithes are mere supports [asmakhta], like the rabbinic Shabbat prohibitions that the Torat Kohanim supports from “a solemn rest” (Beitza 36b). They explain apparent counterproofs: the priest who eats an untithed fig and is flogged (Makkot 19b) receives rabbinic lashes for rebelliousness; a cake of figs that is not nullified (Yevamot 81a) is because the Rabbis made it like Torah law; “grain” including legumes in Nedarim 55a follows common speech in vows (Rabbeinu Tam); the dispute of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua in Ḥullin 120b can concern Torah law, such as liquid squeezed from crushed ears (Shabbat 19a); and “death” for one who eats a teruma fig that fell into the water of purification (Mishna Para 11:3) means a stringent rabbinic penalty, or the fig is a mere example, since teruma of grain, wine and oil is Torah law. The Jerusalem Talmud (beginning of Ma’asrot) seems to treat the inclusion of legumes and fruit as a full derivation and says that only vegetables are tithed “by their words” (Isi ben Akavya); Tosafot explain that this means vegetables have no scriptural support at all, unlike legumes and other fruit. The Sifrei and Torat Kohanim likewise bring no verse for vegetables, perhaps because the Sages were more lenient with vegetables, as in the Jerusalem Talmud (Ḥalla, chapter Shtei Nashim): the sages in the Diaspora separated teruma and tithes until the “rovim” abolished them, and some said they were concerned only for teruma of grain, wine and oil, or only for great teruma, but not at all for vegetables. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
gershom:a4.1: And other species in general, such as beans and lentils: from where do we derive that one does not tithe from one for the other?
gershom:a5.1: If that is so: since you derived that one does not tithe from one species for another that is not its species from “all the best” written twice, that is, give “best” for this one and “best” for that one,
gershom:a6.1: with regard to animal tithe, where “tithe … tithe” is not written twice, since it is not written “tithe of the herd and tithe of the flock,” so too let them be tithed from one for the other.
rashi:b1.1: Let them be tithed from one for the other: cattle and sheep.
rashi:b1.2: The verse states “the tenth”: [the word] “tithe” is attached to the herd and “the tenth” is attached to the flock, so that now a “tithe” is written for each one.
rashi:b1.3: Sheep and goats too: should not be tithed [one for the other], just as above, where “best” is written for the oil and “best” for the wine and grain, and we expound grain [and] grain by an a fortiori inference from wine and oil; so too here we would expound an a fortiori inference from new and old.
rashi:b1.4: And he answers: “or the flock” means all flock is one.
gershom:b1.1: He replied: the verse states “the tenth”; it is as though “tithe … tithe” were written twice.
gershom:b2.1: If so, sheep and goats too: let us say, give a tenth for this one and a tenth for that one, and they should not be tithed one for the other.
gershom:b3.1: But it is written “or the flock,” which means all flock is one.
rashi:b2.1: The first part of them: next to “grain” comes “the first part of them,” to say: give a first part for each and every grain. [It is] in the portion of Koraḥ.
tosafot:b2.1: In brief: Tosafot find this difficult. In Temura 5a, on Abaye’s principle that whatever the Torah forbids is effective if done, the Gemara cites one who separates teruma from one kind for another, which is not teruma, and answers from “the first part of them,” applying it even to wine and oil, to teach that it is not effective; here it is applied to dividing kinds of grain. And Rava here says that even without “the first part of them” one cannot say that “grain” means all grain is one, while there he says explicitly that without “the first part of them” one would have said that wine and grain, with only one “best” written for them, may be separated one for the other. They answer: for Abaye, “the first part” certainly divides kinds of grain, since the verse places it next to “and grain”; he also applies it to teach that it is not effective, since it refers to all the kinds in the verse: for wine and oil it was needed only for that, and just as it is not effective for wine and oil, so too for kinds of grain. Rava here does not need it, since it follows from the a fortiori inference above, and “grain” cannot mean “all grain is one” because it is needed to exclude other species; there it is derived from “the first part” as something that follows from an a fortiori inference which the verse nevertheless bothers to write (Pesaḥim 18b). This also explains why here “the first part” is brought for grain and grain and there for grain and wine: both follow from the a fortiori inference, and the verse wrote it for both. And if you ask why, for Rava, “best … best” is needed, since “the first part of them” refers to them all: because we would not have applied “the first part of them” to wine and oil, since they are not diverse kinds with each other. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
gershom:b4.1: Here too let us say: “all the best of the wine and of the grain,” “all” meaning like one grain, and wheat should be tithed for barley.
gershom:b5.1: The first part of them: give a first part for this one and a first part for that one, so that they are not tithed one for the other.
rashi:b3.1: Granted, there we expound that “or the flock” means all flock is one: since the verses are superfluous for us.
rashi:b3.2: For if it enters your mind that sheep and goats too: may not be tithed one for the other, let the Merciful One write “and all the animal tithe,” and I would know that one species may not [be tithed] for another not its species, since it follows by an a fortiori inference from new and old.
gershom:b6.1: For if it enters your mind that sheep and goats too may not be tithed one for the other, let it write “all the animal tithe” and not write “herd and flock.”
rashi:b4.1: And if you would say: if it had written “animal,” I would say that an undomesticated animal is included in “animal,” and an undomesticated animal would be subject to tithe, as we hold in Bava Kamma (54b) that an undomesticated animal is included in “animal” with regard to crossbreeding; and for that reason [one might think] it had to write “herd and flock.” [No,] for I learn “under,” “under” from sacrificial animals: it is written here “under the rod” (Leviticus 27:32) and there “under its mother” (Leviticus 22:27), and there undomesticated animals are not included, since it is written “a bull, a sheep or a goat.” Therefore let it write “animal,” and it would follow by an a fortiori inference from new and old that one species may not [be tithed] for another not its species; and so it wrote “herd and flock” to say that it is herd and flock that are not tithed one for the other, but flock and flock are tithed. But here, with grain, it is not reasonable to expound the verse to mean that it is wine and grain that are not tithed one for the other while grain and grain are tithed, for could it possibly not have written “grain,” [which is needed] to exclude other species, so that they are not subject to tithe by Torah law?
gershom:b7.1: I would say even an undomesticated animal: just as we derive an undomesticated animal from a domesticated one with regard to crossbreeding, so too one would derive an undomesticated animal for tithe. That cannot be said, since tithe is derived from sacrificial animals by “under … under,” and there are no undomesticated animals among the offerings. So still let it write “all the animal tithe,” and it would follow by an a fortiori inference from new and old: if new and old, which are not diverse kinds with each other, are not tithed one for the other, then sheep and goats, which are diverse kinds with each other, is it not logical that they should not be tithed one for the other? Why do I need “herd and flock,” etc.
tosafot:b5.1: And it would follow by an a fortiori inference from new and old: he could not say that it follows from the juxtaposition of “you shall tithe a tithe” above, since Rava said above: “I juxtaposed them with regard to the year, and not with regard to another matter.”
gershom:b8.1: These sheep and goats are tithed one for the other: that is what “or the flock” comes for, since “all” means one flock, and that is why it is superfluous.
gershom:b9.1: But here, would it suffice if it did not write “grain,” to exclude other species: which are not subject to tithe by Torah law? It is not superfluous, to say that all [grain] tithe is one grain.
rashi:b7.1: Say: to intermingle herd with flock: that is, from where does Rava know that “herd and flock” is written so that they should not be tithed one for the other? Say that the verse specified them explicitly in order to intermingle them, so that they would be tithed one for the other: for had it written “animal,” we would derive from new and old that one species may not [be tithed] for another not its species, and therefore it mentioned them explicitly, to say that they should be tithed one for the other. And Rav Huna presumed that since Rava does not hold of “the first part of them,” he also does not hold of “the tenth,” to expound “give a tenth for this one and a tenth for that one,” since it is not written “tithe of the herd and tithe of the flock.”
tosafot:b7.1: Say: to intermingle them in the flock: since it wrote them under a single “tithe,” and did not write “and the tithe of the flock.”
gershom:b10.1: Say: to intermingle them, herd with flock: this “or the flock” that it wrote was not written to teach that sheep are tithed for goats, but to intermingle herd with flock, so that one tithes from the herd for the flock and from the flock for the herd.
gershom:b11.1: Rava too, who derives from “or the flock” that it means all flock [is one], also holds of “the tenth”: give a tenth for the herd and a tenth for the flock.
rashi:b8.1: From one species for another that is not its species, no: and if you say, [then] sheep and goats too [should not be tithed together], what, then, does the amplification of “herd and flock” accomplish? And if you say, what did you see [to apply them this way]? It is reasonable that the juxtaposition comes to exclude herd and flock, so that they are not tithed one for the other, since they are not similar to each other at all, and the amplification of “herd and flock” comes to include sheep and goats, since they are similar to each other with regard to offerings: one who says “I take upon myself [an offering] from the flock” may bring either a sheep or a goat.
rashi:b9.1: Rava retracted from that one: the first one, and holds that it is juxtaposed for other matters too, to exclude herd with flock; and that sheep and goats are tithed [together] we derive from the amplification of “herd and flock.” And when we asked at the beginning of the discussion [53b], “If so, new and old too,” that is no refutation, since for new and old the verse explicitly writes that they are juxtaposed, for in the verse of the juxtaposition “year, year” is written.
tosafot:b9.1: One of them was said by Rav Pappa: so too it says at the beginning of Bava Kamma (4b). It is usual to say this of Rav Pappa, since he presided after Rava, as is stated in Mo’ed Katan (28b), and there are things he said that people thought were said in Rava’s name.
rashi:b10.1: Mishna. Joins together within the range of the foot of a grazing animal: according to the measure that an animal moves away as it goes grazing, which is sixteen mil. Another version: according to how far apart the animals can be from each other and still be watched by one shepherd, which is sixteen mil, as the Gemara explains, for that is how far a shepherd’s eye reaches. If he has five animals in this village and five animals in another village sixteen mil from it, he brings them into one pen and tithes them; and if they are farther apart, they are exempt. The Gemara explains the reason.
gershom:b12.1: Joins together within the range of the foot of a grazing animal: that is, all the animals of one person that graze in one field, within the distance that an animal’s foot goes while grazing, so that one shepherd can guard them, join together to be tithed together, since it is one herd.
gershom:b13.1: Sixteen mil: for the Rabbis have an accepted tradition that an animal’s foot goes no farther than that, and all that stand within sixteen mil join together.
rashi:b10.2: Thirty-two mil: the Gemara asks what it means.
gershom:b14.1: If he had two herds, and between these and those there were thirty-two mil, they do not join together.
rashi:b10.3: If he had in the middle: those in the middle join the sides together; and when it teaches “he brings and tithes them in the middle,” it does not mean actually bringing them.
gershom:b15.1: If he had a herd in the middle of those thirty-two [mil], he brings all of them to that herd in the middle and tithes them, since now there are no more than sixteen mil between one herd and the next; but the outer ones he cannot bring to each other, since there are more than sixteen mil between them.
rashi:b10.4: The Jordan divides: if he has five animals on this side and five on that side, with the Jordan between them, they do not join and are exempt; and the Gemara explains the reason.
gershom:b16.1: The Jordan [divides]: they do not join together for one tithe.
rashi:b12.1: Gemara. The flock shall again pass under the hands of him who counts them: this implies that if they can be counted by one shepherd, they are called a flock and “pass under the rod” to be tithed; and if not, not.
gershom:b17.1: Under the hands of him who counts: the shepherd. That is, the flock that one shepherd can guard and count is one herd and joins together for one tithe, for the counting, which is the tithe.
gershom:b18.1: And the Sages have an accepted tradition, etc.: “shall pass” [ta’avorna] is like the expression “whatever passes” [ya’avor] written regarding the tithe.
rashi:b13.1: But it teaches sixteen mil: [within that] they join; more, no.
gershom:b19.1: That is why it teaches thirty-two: because it wants to teach the latter clause, “if he had [animals] in the middle” of those thirty-two; but in one herd, beyond sixteen [mil] they do not join.
rashi:b14.1: And how many: must he have at the sides and in the middle for them to join?
gershom:b20.1: And how many animals must there be in those thirty-two mil, when he has [some] in the middle, for them to join?
rashi:b14.2: Five from here and five in the middle: join together, and he brings them into one pen and tithes them; and the five that remain in the [other] pen join for another threshing floor [i.e., a later round of tithing] when more lambs are born to him. But if those on one side were close to the middle ones, within sixteen mil, and those on the other side were farther than sixteen mil, those far ones are entirely exempt, and need not wait until more lambs are born to him to join for another threshing floor.
rashi:b14.3: For these five: in the middle are fit for here and for there, since whichever side they join, there is the measure for tithe [ten]. But if there are five here and four there and five in the middle, the four do not join, and need not wait for another threshing floor.
rashi:b15.1: Five from here and five from there and one in the middle: even though this one is not fit for the count [it cannot make ten with either side], since the shepherd’s way is to go there and bring it, it is as though he stands there, and we apply to him “him who counts.” And all the more so four from here and five from there and one in the middle, where this one is fit to join for the count.
